title: Average hash (aHash) — Reverse Image Matching
description: aHash shrinks any image to 8x8 grayscale, then sets each bit by whether the pixel beats the mean. The 64-bit result is a fingerprint: resizes and recompression barely move it. Hamming distance between fingerprints ranks near-duplicates in microseconds.

title: Perceptual hash (pHash) — Reverse Image Matching
description: pHash applies a discrete cosine transform to the shrunken grayscale image and keeps the low-frequency coefficients. Low frequencies encode structure while ignoring fine noise, making pHash sturdier than aHash under edits. It is the workhorse hash for finding copies across re-encodes and resizes.
provenance: Public methodology — standard computer-science technique documented in the technical literature; fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: Difference hash (dHash) — Reverse Image Matching
description: dHash compares each pixel to its right neighbor instead of the global mean, encoding gradients. Gradient bits survive brightness and contrast shifts that can flip aHash bits. dHash is often the best cheap hash for photographic near-duplicates.
provenance: Public methodology — standard computer-science technique documented in the technical literature; fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: Hamming distance ranking — Reverse Image Matching
description: Two 64-bit hashes compare by Hamming distance: the count of differing bit positions. Distance 0-5 means near-certain duplicates; 6-10 means likely variants; beyond that, unrelated. Threshold choice trades recall of edited copies against precision.
provenance: Public methodology — standard computer-science technique documented in the technical literature; fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: Block-based matching — Reverse Image Matching
description: When only part of an image matches, block hashes fingerprint overlapping tiles independently. A query tile hitting any gallery tile flags the containing image, catching crops and composites. Block matching finds images that global hashes miss entirely.

title: Keypoint-verified matches — Reverse Image Matching
description: Hash candidates are verified by matching SIFT-style keypoints with geometric consistency checks. RANSAC finds the transform aligning the most keypoint pairs, rejecting coincidental hash hits. Verification turns fast-but-loose hash retrieval into court-grade matching.

title: Handling transformations — Reverse Image Matching
description: Copies arrive rotated, flipped, cropped, or recolored; robust pipelines hash multiple normalized variants. Some systems store hashes for the four rotations and both flips, covering the common edits. Each variant costs one more hash comparison, cheap next to the retrieval value.

description: Web-scale reverse search shards hash indexes by hash prefix so each query touches one shard. Multi-index hashing splits 64-bit codes into blocks, finding all near neighbors without full scans. Sharding plus multi-indexing keeps billion-image lookup interactive.
